https://www.theguardian.com/uk-news/2026.text: Sally-Anne Bowen arriving at Harrow crown court. Photograph: James Manning/PA View image in fullscreen Sally-Anne Bowen arriving at Harrow crown court. Photograph: James Manning/PA Crime Woman found guilty of indecent assault against two pupils at London boys’ school in 1980s Sally-Anne Bowen, now 65, convicted of assaulting boys at Christ’s College, Finchley, where she was chemistry teacher Caroline Davies and agency Thu 27 Aug 2026 13.23 EDT Last modified on Thu 27 Aug 2026 15.32 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google A chemistry teacher has been found guilty of indecently assaulting two teenage pupils at an all-boys school in the late 1980s. Sally-Anne Bowen, who taught at Christ’s College in Finchley, north London , assaulted the teenage boys when they were aged around 14 to 15 and she was in her mid-20s. Bowen, of Hemel Hempstead, Hertfordshire, did not appear to show any emotion as a jury at Harrow crown court returned majority verdicts finding the 65-year-old guilty of seven counts of indecent assault after six hours and 29 minutes of deliberations. One complainant told jurors he had sex with the teacher “about 20 or 30 times” over several months. He would visit Bowen’s home, considered her to be his girlfriend and had fallen in love, the court heard. In his evidence, the man – who cannot be named for legal reasons – said he kept their relationship secret because he felt compelled to protect the teacher, who he said had drummed it into him that he was not allowed to tell anyone. “I never, ever spoke to anyone about it,” he said. “I was always really aware, she drummed it into me.” He added: “Years she got to teach because I remained silent.” He said in a police interview that the experience had been “the destruction of my education”. Madeleine Wolfe, prosecuting, told jurors in her closing speech that the man’s evidence had “a real visceral quality to it”. She said: “There can be no doubt that there was a lasting impact on him. It’s not a schoolboy fantasy, is it? He’s started this account in 2014 – this has real-life implications for him, remained with him for decades.” It was not until he became a parent himself that the man began to realise what had happened to him, Wolfe said. The second complainant said he and Bowen kissed once in a cafe when he was goaded into it by other boys. Another former pupil at the school, Tobias Oliver, said during the trial that Bowen acted as if she was in “a Sabrina Carpenter video” while in the classroom, and “dressed and behaved more like my teenage female friends than the other teachers”. Oliver, who did not know the two victims, told jurors: “The topics of conversation in class often strayed away from chemistry and became quite sexual.” Bowen had no boundaries and “felt more like trying to be one of us, like our friend, than a teacher,” he said. Bowen was “very flirtatious” in class and told them how she enjoyed giving oral sex to her boyfriend, he said. He recalled an occasion when a boy in Bowen’s class was reading a “sex manual”, which he believed to be the Kama Sutra. He said Bowen went through the book and discussed “the merits of different sexual positions” with the students. Oliver also described how on another occasion Bowen sat on a desk and caught the attention of the class before slowly opening her legs, revealing her underwear. Richard Luker, who was head of science at the school in the late 1980s, told the court he remembered a complaint from the first victim’s mother that she was concerned the boy was planning to travel abroad with Bowen at the end of term. During the trial, Bowen claimed the allegations were “total fabrication”. She said she had had a medical condition that in the late 1980s had not been diagnosed and had made sexual intercourse difficult and painful for her. Her partner of 36 years, Darren Scotchbrook, giving evidence, said Bowen had not been aware of her condition when they met in 1990, and sex had been “clearly not enjoyable for her” as a result. Asked under cross-examination how she had dressed in the classroom, Bowen replied that she “wasn’t going to dress like Margaret Thatcher” in her mid-20s. She told the court she did not flirt with students and was “just friendly”. She denied having a relationship with the first complainant. “Absolutely not, no relationship whatsoever. Student-teacher,” she said. She denied knowing the second complainant, saying she did not remember him even after seeing him give evidence in court. Allegations against Bowen featured in the Tortoise Investigates podcast Lucky Boy last year. Bowen was granted bail until her sentence hearing on 20 November. https://thecolu.mn/4552/allegation-maja-.text: Politics August 14, 2026 Allegation: Maja T. in Custody for Wearing a Dress Belonging to Guards The nonbinary German person Maja T. says they were mistreated by guards because of their gender identity. According to the newspaper nd, a supporters’ group reported a violent assault by exclusively male correctional officers in a men’s prison in Budapest. The incident was reportedly triggered by Maja T. wearing a dress. Five guards allegedly stripped the inmate, forcefully and violently. Hungarian authorities justified the action by stating that “women’s clothing” is prohibited in men’s penal facilities. Maja T. now faces a disciplinary proceeding for the incident, which could lead to renewed isolation. Human rights organizations condemn such measures as “extermination detention,” a practice aimed at breaking the will to live of an incarcerated person. Maja T. has long argued that, as a nonbinary person, they face discrimination in Hungarian custody. Lawmakers from several factions in the German Bundestag sent an open letter to Foreign Minister Johann Wadephul (CDU) in June, urging him to press for the person’s transfer — but so far without success (TheColu.mn reported). Fragwürdige Verurteilung  und Versagen der deutschen Behörden The Budapest City Court sentenced Maja T. in February of this year to eight years in prison after an evidentiary process (TheColu.mn reported). At the time, the authoritarian-leaning Prime Minister Viktor Orbán and high-ranking members of his government publicly called for a harsh punishment and explicitly demanded that the judge make an example of the nonbinary person. Judge József Sós concluded that it was proven the 25-year-old person from the left-wing scene in Germany participated in bloody assaults on alleged right-wing extremists in Budapest. About 20 German and other alleged left-wing extremists were said to have injured nine people, four seriously. Supporters of T. describe this as a political trial. In theory, T. should not have been extradited from Germany to Hungary. The German Federal Constitutional Court had blocked this in a provisional order. German authorities, according to their supporters, sought to remove T. quickly in a “night and fog” operation, so the order from Karlsruhe reached the responsible agency 50 minutes after T. had been handed over to Hungary (TheColu.mn reported). Later the court deemed the extradition inadmissible — the Kammergericht did not thoroughly examine general deficiencies in Hungarian detention facilities or concerns about safety and discrimination of the nonbinary person (TheColu.mn reported). The federal government has since made no publicly known efforts to rectify this injustice. Marcy Ellerton My name is Marcy Ellerton, and I’ve been telling stories since I could hold a pen. As a queer journalist based in Minneapolis, I cover everything from grassroots activism to the everyday moments that make our community shine. When I’m not chasing a story, you’ll probably find me in a coffee shop, scribbling notes in a well-worn notebook and eavesdropping just enough to catch the next lead. Latest Post

https://telex.hu/kulfold/2026/09/14/szic.text: Menü Kereső Több mint hét évet kaptak a magyar nőket szexuálisan bántalmazó marokkói bevándorlók Olaszországban Külföld Pál Tamás Állítsd be a Telexet megbízható forrásnak! Beállítom A cataniai büntetőbíróság első fokon 7 év és 2 hónap börtönbüntetésre ítélt két marokkói férfit, akik tavaly szexuális erőszakot követtek el két magyar nő ellen Szicíliában. Egy harmadik elkövető 7 év 4 hónap börtönt kapott – írta az MTI. A 23 és 26 év közötti férfiakat csoportosan elkövetett szexuális erőszak , valamint kábítószer-birtoklás és drogfogyasztásra kényszerítés miatt ítélték el. Az ügy gyorsított eljárással zajlott, így az eredetileg kiszabható büntetés egyharmadát elengedték. Az elkövetőket a tavalyi elfogásuk óta külön börtönökben tartják fogva. Az ítélet felolvasásakor jelen voltak, de nem kaptak szót a bírósági döntés bejelentése után. A bűncselekmény elkövetésekor mind a három marokkói állampolgár illegális bevándorlóként tartózkodott Olaszországban, azonban ebben az eljárásban nem kaptak büntetést. A magyar nőknek járó kártérítésről a bíróság külön döntést hoz. Az összeghez az erőszak áldozatai számára létrehozott olasz állami alap is hozzájárul. A két magyar nőt képviselő Massimiliano Scaringella ügyvéd az MTI-nek azt mondta, elégedett, mivel jelentős ítéletről van szó, amely megerősítette az elvet, hogy ilyesmi Olaszországban nem történhet meg. „Ilyen magatartás nem tűrhető el, és nem is fogadják el. A bíróság teljes mértékben hitelesnek tartotta az erőszakot elszenvedett fiatal nők beszámolóját” – mondta. A két áldozat a tárgyalásokon nem vett részt, ügyvédjük szerint a magánéletük védelmében távol kívántak maradni. Az erőszakról a La Sicilia napilap számolt be először. A magyar nők tavaly augusztus utolsó napjaiban Catania tengerpartjánál elfogadtak egy fuvart a szállásukra a két vádlottól, akik azonban ehelyett egy távol eső helyre vitték őket, ahol a harmadik társuk is csatlakozott hozzájuk. Ezután kokain fogyasztására és szexuális cselekményekre kényszerítették őket. A rendőrségnek sikerült a csoportot Paterno településén lenyomoznia, köszönhetően az egyik áldozat lánytestvérének, aki eltűntként jelentette a két fiatal nőt, és aktivált egy telefonos nyomkövető szolgáltatást, amellyel sikerült lokalizálni az egyikük mobilját. Korábban Sebastiano Ardita cataniai ügyészhelyettes az MTI-nek azt mondta, hogy a marokkói férfiaknak az ítéletet követően le kell tölteniük a börtönbüntetést, erre Olaszországban vagy Marokkóban is sor kerülhet, ha Marokkó garantálja, hogy letöltik a teljes büntetést. Ardita hozzátette, hogy az olasz hatóságok prioritásként kezelik a szexuális erőszak büntetését, és azt mondta, az olasz büntető törvénykönyv nem tesz különbséget szexuális erőszak és szexuális agresszió elnevezés között. https://www.theguardian.com/australia-ne.text: Victoria has banned gas in all new homes from 1 January. A major natural gas distribution network operator has claimed ‘voters hate the ban’, as it lobbies the state government to reverse the measure. Photograph: Elena Popova/Getty Images View image in fullscreen Victoria has banned gas in all new homes from 1 January. A major natural gas distribution network operator has claimed ‘voters hate the ban’, as it lobbies the state government to reverse the measure. Photograph: Elena Popova/Getty Images Victorian politics Gas lobby ‘scare campaign’ urges Victoria to scrap ban in new homes, leaked documents show Exclusive: Australian Gas Infrastructure Group lobbying campaign warns energy bills could increase by $100 unless ban is reversed, despite experts disagreeing Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast Henry Belot Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.00 EDT Last modified on Wed 23 Sep 2026 11.02 EDT Share Prefer the Guardian on Google The gas industry has been accused of unleashing a “scare campaign” before the Victorian election as it pressures the state government to reverse a ban on gas in new homes . A paper prepared by a lobbyist for the Australian Gas Infrastructure Group (AGIG) and shared with ministers has warned annual household gas bills could increase by $100 unless the ban is overturned, without providing evidence to support that claim. From 1 January, all new homes and commercial buildings cannot be connected to the gas network and must instead run on electricity. The government expects this could save households $880 a year – or $1,820 once solar panels are installed. New gasfield approved near Twelve Apostles puts climate and ‘pristine’ ocean in jeopardy, environmentalists warn Read more AGIG – which is owned by a Hong-Kong led consortium – operates and owns major natural gas distribution networks and pipelines in Victoria . The company’s business model will be hit when new homes are not connected to these networks. The document obtained by Guardian Australia was written by AGIG’s lobbyist, Ken McAlpine, and provides detailed advice on how regulation should be changed, how the ban could be reversed before the election, and how it should be announced to the media. The document also provides unsolicited political advice claiming a change would neutralise a “key opposition attack line”. The Coalition has pledged to repeal the ban. McAlpine also cites unnamed qualitative research to claim “voters hate the ban”. Sign up for the Breaking News Australia email The document cites modelling that suggests the government’s ban would lead to a network cost increase of 20% to 40% “primarily due to demand and customer reductions” associated with the ban. The document claims small businesses and industrial customers could see gas price increases of more than $100 a year. “AGIG is currently discussing these price increases with customer representatives as part of their regulator price reset process, but these numbers will likely become public by mid-September,” the document says. The numbers have not yet been made public. Tony Wood, an energy and climate change senior fellow at the Grattan Institute, said the document was “clearly a scare campaign”. “I do not understand why there would be any price increases,” Wood said. In March 2025, AGIG told the state government that network costs would increase for remaining gas customers as more people moved to electric homes. “We have been warning against that outcome for some time and it should not be allowed,” Wood said. “The consumers who will be ‘forced’ to go electric rather than have a gas connection will be financially better off.” skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | When needed Sign up to Breaking News Australia Get the most important news as it breaks after newsletter promotion An AGIG spokesperson said the document was not written by the group but that it reflected its submissions to government and its campaigning on this issue. Environment Victoria’s chief executive, Jonathan La Nauze, said the letter’s foreshadowing of a price increase – which is set by the independent Australian Energy Regulator and not AGIG – agreed the document was indicative of a “scare campaign”. “This shows a sophisticated campaign that has considered the political and policy mechanisms,” La Nauze said. “They are very, very focused on getting what they want before caretaker period begins. “I would absolutely urge and expect Ben Carroll to put the interests of Victorians before the interests of a foreign-owned private gas company.” When asked about the lobbying document, the Victorian minister for energy and resources, Jaclyn Symes, said the government’s position “has not changed”. “We’ve always said gas is part of our energy transition – but the reality is legacy supplies from Victoria’s Bass Strait are dwindling and prices are going up,” Symes said. Francis Vierboom, chief executive officer of the non-profit Rewiring Australia, said AGIG was “trying to do the department’s homework for them”. “We need to make sure that the government is taking its own advice and following the sensible and nation-leading policies they have already announced,” Vierboom said. The leader of the Victorian Greens, Ellen Sandell, said “the gas lobby has become so brazen it’s literally written the government a step-by-step playbook for watering down the rules, right down to the media release it wants Labor to send”. https://www.dw.com/en/spain-floods-leave.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5NhNf The flooding wreaked havoc on the town of Madrigueras in Spain's Castilla-La Mancha region Image: Eva Manez/REUTERS Advertisement Floods in the Spanish southeastern town of Madrigueras have killed an 102-year-old woman, regional authorities said. Madrigueras, which has a population of around 4,000 residents, is located near the city of Albacete in the Spanish autonomous community of Castilla-La Mancha. Authorities said 90 people had to be rescued due to flooding in the town. Local Spanish media said the elderly woman was found dead in her home after the floodwaters had reached a depth of one meter (3.2 feet). The floods in the region were caused by persistent torrential rainfall on Friday. Spanish authorities said around 140 liters of rainfall per square meter came down in Madrigueras. The flooding in Madrigueras also damaged vehicles in the town Image: Eva Manez/REUTERS Sanchez: Spanish government monitoring flood situation Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez , in a post on X, said his government is monitoring the situation. He also expressed his regards to the family of the woman who died in the flooding in Madrigueras. Spanish meteorological authorities said heavy rainfall is expected to continue in eastern Spain through Sunday. The torrential rain and flooding comes after the Mediterranean country witnessed its hottest summer on record this year. Deadly wildfires were reported in Spain's north and south in recent months due to frequent hot , dry conditions. Viewpoints Opinion Conrad Black: France Has a Long History of Rowdy Mass Protests Save Mark Us Preferred on Google Print Turned-over cars cover Gay-Lussac Street in Paris on the morning of May 11, 1968, after violent fights between students and police the night before. AFP via Getty Images Conrad Black 10/6/2026 | Updated: 10/6/2026 0:00 X 1 Commentary The riots in France are following a traditional pattern in that country. It is a part of the political nature of the French republics that every 20 or 30 years, discontent suddenly bubbles up uncontrollably. All who know France know that it is a beautiful country with magnificent landscapes almost everywhere, where the French language is spoken beautifully even by apparently uneducated people, and where it is almost impossible to get a bad meal or a poor glass of wine. From Gen. Charles de Gaulle’s founding of his Fifth Republic in 1958 up until the 1980s, the per capita French standard of living rose steadily to about 90 percent of the American average. It has dwindled from there to about 72 percent. The public sector share of the GDP is approximately 57 percent , more than 20 points higher than the United States, even with its immense military establishment. There are identifiable causes for this comparatively undistinguished performance. But underlying it all is the ancient cleavage between the French rankling under any sort of authority and who at the same time have a bourgeois dislike of anything that costs them money. Like a reliable geyser, the French rise up every generation or so and for a time hurl paving stones at the police, pile up barricades in the streets, set cars and piles of garbage on fire, and obstruct normal movement. A classic case of this tendency, still within the memory of many people including myself, was the famous events of May 1968. The president, de Gaulle, was in Romania at the time urging that country to slough off the yoke of the Soviet Union while the prime minister, Georges Pompidou, was selling the Gaullist message in, of all places, Afghanistan. University students marched out of their classes, denouncing conditions in the universities and in the country generally. Their antics stirred up a sympathetic response from organized labor, and a general strike was announced by the private and public sector unions. De Gaulle and Pompidou returned in due course, and de Gaulle departed Paris for his country home at Colombey-les-Deux-Églises 180 kilometres east of the city. There he remained, in sphinx-like incommunicability, for two weeks as disorder reigned around the country, garbage wasn’t collected, and the fun of the chaos gradually declined. The Paris police chief told the prime minister that he could no longer be sure of the loyalty of his force. Rumours were rife that de Gaulle was about to resign. The BBC headlined its world newscast in the midst of these events with ill-concealed cheerfulness: “Day by day, we see the proud facade of Gaullism crumbling into dust.” Firefighters extinguish a fire outside Jean-Louis Cyffle high school during a nationwide student protest over learning conditions in Nancy, France, on Oct. 5, 2026. Jean-Christophe Verhaegen / AFP via Getty Images Finally, it was announced that de Gaulle had visited the commander of the main French army, the Army of the Rhine, was returning to Paris, and would address the nation the following day. Rumors circulated that he had assured himself of the loyalty of the army for any contingency, while the left, which had completely prevailed in the public discourse for weeks, predicted the president’s resignation. When de Gaulle spoke to the country, the state radio and television network was on strike and all viewers got was a still picture of him, though his voice was transmitted accurately. He had judged exactly when the French love of disorder and fundamental dislike for authority would give way to the avaricious bourgeois concern that these antics might actually cost them something. Related Stories Conrad Black: Why This Year’s UN Session Was Different Conrad Black: Greenland Deal Is Good News for the Western Alliance De Gaulle spoke for only eight minutes. “As the holder of the legitimacy of the nation and of the Republic, I have over the past 24 hours considered every eventuality, without exception, which would permit me to maintain that legitimacy. I have made my resolutions,” he said. “In the present circumstances, I will not step down. I have a mandate from the people, and I will fulfill it. I will not change the prime minister, whose value, soundness, and capacity merit the tribute of all. … I am today dissolving the National Assembly. … As for the general elections, these will be held within the period provided for under the Constitution (which he had written), unless there is an intention to gag the entire French people to prevent them from expressing their views as they are being prevented from carrying on their lives, by the same methods being used to prevent students from studying, teachers from teaching, workers from working. … France is threatened with dictatorship. There are those who would constrain her to abandon herself to a power that would establish itself in national despair, a power that would then obviously and essentially be the power of totalitarian communism.” (He was referring to former premier Maurice Mendès-France and future president Francois Mitterrand.) It was clear that the public right to vote would be upheld by whatever means of force was necessary, and that de Gaulle would not hesitate to assume emergency powers, as the Constitution permitted. At midday on the day of de Gaulle’s speech, 500,000 people marched up the Champs-Élysées demanding his resignation. He spoke at the end of the afternoon, and 90 minutes later a March of over 700,000 proceeded back down the Champs-Élysées demanding that he remain. The strikes collapsed. The bourgeois spirit of France asserted itself; all violence ended. Everyone went back to work and to their place of study, and on election day in June, de Gaulle won the greatest victory in the 175 intermittent years of French democracy through all five republics. (Mendès-France and Mitterrand suffered personal defeat.) As in 1944 when he outsmarted the communists after the Liberation, and in 1958 and 1962 when civil war threatened from Algeria, de Gaulle again completely routed the left. The current French president, Emmanuel Macron, has nothing like the prestige or record of achievement of Charles de Gaulle, but as he demonstrated in the “yellow vest” disturbances of several years ago (disorder on the right caused by increased costs and taxes as a result of excessive climate change measures), he is little inclined to bow to rioters. The students, unlike the workers, are a shower: easy to disperse and little supported by public sympathy, given the money society deluges on them. As of now, there’s no sign that the workers’ organizations are inclined to make the current protest a general strike, which would re-create a 1968 scenario. But it is clear that this disorder is being encouraged by the ultra-left coalition France Undefeated (“La France Insoumise”), and the conservative Ralliement National led by Marine Le Pen is steadily strengthening its position in the polls. Whatever happens, this is another nail in the coffin of the overbearing federal Eurostate, and the companion causes of social democratic, Davos-like government. For Prime Minister Mark Carney and Canada, such an approach would be like boarding a ship that cannot sail and will sink if it tries. https://www.dw.com/en/will-guinea-bissau.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5OYTN Soldiers patrol the main street in Bissau, the capital of Guinea-Bissau. Following the 2025 military coup, the country's state institutions were suspended Image: Luc Gnago/REUTERS Advertisement The parliamentary and presidential elections scheduled for December 6, 2026, in Guinea-Bissau will not take place as planned. Aly Silva, spokesperson for transitional Prime Minister Ilidio Vieira Te, confirmed to DW that the vote had been postponed until further notice. No new date has been set. The government first intends to discuss the matter in cabinet before publicly announcing when the elections will be held. It remains unclear whether they will take place in 2027 or not until 2028. The country's political crisis dates back to November 26, 2025. Three days earlier, voters in Guinea-Bissau had elected a new parliament and president. Before the official results could be announced, the military seized power and halted the electoral process. Both then-President Umaro Sissoco Embalo and his challenger, Fernando Dias da Costa, had claimed victory. The military leadership promised a return to constitutional order. Guinea-Bissau's General Horta N'Tam (center) was sworn in as transitional leader and commander-in-chief on November 27, 2025 Image: Patrick Meinhardt/AFP For lawyer and political analyst Cabi Sanha, the postponement comes as no surprise. Since the coup, little has been done to create the conditions for credible elections, he says. "The postponement was foreseeable," Sanha told DW. December 6 had indeed been set as the new election date. "But nothing was done to ensure that these elections could actually take place." Political freedoms under pressure The transitional government has justified the postponement by citing the lack of organizational and political conditions necessary for elections. The deadline for submitting candidacies had already passed on October 6. Political parties and potential candidates had not submitted their applications. According to the prime minister, the parties had also failed to hold congresses to select their candidates. Sanha sees this as more than an organizational problem. He points to restrictions on political activities and the lack of dialogue with key actors in the electoral process. Political parties and civil society have not been sufficiently involved, he says. Mediation efforts by the Economic Community of West African States (ECOWAS) and Senegal have so far failed to produce a solution. "Free, transparent and inclusive elections are only possible if the necessary conditions are established beforehand," the lawyer says. He therefore also views the parties' failure to nominate candidates as a consequence of the political environment. "How are parties supposed to nominate candidates when political activities are restricted in the country? They cannot hold party congresses or organize rallies." The funeral of human rights activist Vigario Balanta in Bissau, Guinea-Bissau. His body was found on March 31, bearing signs of torture, in a swamp outside the capital Image: DW Leading opposition figures are also staying abroad. Domingos Simoes Pereira, head of the main opposition party, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde (PAIGC), was allowed to travel to Portugal in July 2026 for medical treatment after being released from detention . He had previously been held in pretrial detention in connection with an investigation into an alleged coup attempt. His defense team denies the allegations and has criticized the proceedings as politically motivated. The absence of key opposition figures and restrictions on political organizing are making it harder to conduct an electoral process intended to pave the way for a return to civilian government. An election date without a timetable What happens next remains unclear. Government spokesperson Aly Silva says the transitional government will first discuss the matter in cabinet. Only afterward will a new election date be announced publicly. So far, there is no concrete timetable. It is therefore also unclear when political parties will be able to complete their internal selection procedures, nominate candidates and begin campaigning. For Sanha, this is another indication that there is still insufficient evidence of the political will needed to restore constitutional order. "I do not believe that logistical problems are the main issue. Rather, there appears to be a lack of political will to move the electoral process forward," he says. Dispute over the constitution The political crisis has been compounded by a controversial constitutional reform. In a referendum on August 30, 2026, voters approved constitutional amendments that expand the president's powers and reduce the size of parliament from 102 to 65 seats. Critics question the legitimacy of the process because the reform was prepared under military rule and without a regularly elected parliament. The opposition had called for a boycott of the vote. Fernando Vaz, spokesperson for the National Transitional Council, defends the changes. He says the process was not a comprehensive rewriting of the constitution but a targeted revision. The reform is intended to help overcome the country's political instability, he argues. "The constitution must be one of the instruments that lead our country toward greater stability," Vaz told DW. The transitional period had provided an opportunity to amend provisions that, in the military leadership's view, were obstructing the country's political development. Vaz also rejects criticism that the reform gives the president additional powers at the expense of the prime minister. "The president of the republic is the head of state, while the prime minister is the head of government," he emphasizes. Critics see it differently. The new constitutional framework strengthens the presidency: the president is to appoint and dismiss the prime minister and the government and, under certain conditions, dissolve parliament. At the same time, the number of parliamentary seats is being reduced. It remains disputed whether the reform will genuinely contribute to stability or instead concentrate more power in the presidency. Around 70 percent of valid votes in a constitutional referendum on August 30, 2026, were cast in favor of constitutional amendments Image: DW Local elections are not enough The transitional government has announced plans to hold local elections in 2027. Sanha broadly welcomes the proposal: Guinea-Bissau has never held such elections since independence. Nevertheless, he stresses that they must not replace the outstanding national elections. "First, parliamentary and presidential elections must take place so that the country can return to constitutional order. Local elections can follow afterward," he says. Local elections cannot compensate for the lack of democratic legitimacy at the national level. Political freedoms must also be restored so that parties can select their candidates and voters can genuinely choose between political alternatives. A transition with no clear end Guinea-Bissau has endured decades of political instability, marked by military coups, institutional crises and repeated interruptions of democratic processes. The latest coup continues this pattern. The renewed postponement of the elections shows how far the country remains from a return to constitutional order. Setting a new election date alone will not be enough. Political activities must be permitted again, parties must be included in the process, and reliable conditions for elections must be established, lawyer Cabi Sanha told DW.
